extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in humour, folklore, linguistics, and comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Describing, analysing, and producing verbal jokes: their definitional features, narrative/performative elements, cognitive mechanisms, classification (GTVH), and social/contextual considerations. Useful for scholars, comedians, and anyone studying how jokes work and how audiences respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke is a display of humour in which words are used within a specific and well-defined narrative structure to make people laugh and is usually not meant to be interpreted literally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically takes the form of a story, often with dialogue, and ends in a punchline; distinguished from other forms of humour (practical jokes, slapstick, anecdotes). Useful as a baseline criterion when identifying verbal jokes versus other humorous forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes benefit from brevity, containing no more detail than is needed to set the scene for the punchline at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep only details that lead directly to understanding and decoding the punchline. Exception/anti-pattern: the 'shaggy dog story' deliberately subverts brevity by long, pointless narration that fails to deliver a punchline; such subversion can itself be a source of humour but violates the usual brevity guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline as culmination
rubrics_metrics.description: The funniness culminates in the final sentence, called the punchline; the tension should reach its highest level at the very end and no continuation relieving the tension should be added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design narrative tension to peak at the punchline (Hetzron). Avoid adding post-punchline continuation that dissipates the tension. Punchline is the pivot that reveals the humorous element (could be a pun, irony, sarcasm, hyperbole or logical incompatibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Script opposition / script switching
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour arises when the punchline triggers an abrupt shift from a primary (obvious) interpretation to a secondary, opposing interpretation — i.e., two scripts that are both compatible with the text but opposite or incompatible with each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the joke text supports both scripts up to the punchline; the punchline must enable the audience to switch scripts quickly. This is central to Raskin's Script-based Semantic Theory of Humour (SSTH) and underlies many verbal jokes and puns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Mechanism (LM)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechanism that connects different scripts in the joke, e.g., pun, faulty logic, false analogy, or other devices that enable the script shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an LM appropriate to the scripts and narrative (simple verbal techniques like puns, or more complex logical devices). The LM must plausibly link the two scripts so the switch is perceived and resolved by the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situation (SI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects, activities, instruments, props, settings and contextual elements needed to tell the story and make the scripts plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define situation elements clearly enough to support both scripts; some situations (e.g., lightbulb jokes) strongly constrain possible narrative strategies and LMs. Situation choices affect plausibility and audience recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target (TA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The actor(s) who become the 'butt' of the joke; identifies who or what is being ridiculed or referenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that targets often rely on stereotypes (ethnic, professional, etc.) and that targeting has social functions (ingroup/outgroup signalling). Ethical/social appropriateness and potential offence depend on audience/context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative strategy (NS)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative format of the joke (simple narrative, dialogue, riddle, one-liner, etc.) that organises how the scripts and LM are presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an NS that fits the SI and LM (e.g., a lightbulb joke will typically be a riddle structure). NS affects pacing, timing, and how information is revealed to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (LA)
rubrics_metrics.description: All information necessary for the verbalisation of a text: exact wording and placement of functional elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precise wording and placement are critical; small lexical or syntactic changes can alter script compatibility or block the required shift. LA controls micro-level delivery of setup and punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing / performance frame
rubrics_metrics.description: A (often formulaic) expression or device that keys the audience to expect a joke, creating a social space and clear boundaries around the narrative (e.g., 'Have you heard the one...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use framing to signal play-mode; if the audience does not enter play, the joke may fail. Subject lines and conversational markers serve this role in electronic communication. Framing can elicit anticipation or be dismissed as inappropriate depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell structure: preface, telling, response
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke telling is sequentially organised into preface (framing), the telling (narrative), and the response sequences; telling is a cooperative interaction between teller and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the preface and telling to invite the expected response; allow room for audience acknowledgement and laughter. Tellers often adapt wording on the fly depending on memory and audience reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic timing and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: In performance, comic timing and rhythm (pauses, pacing, physical actions) are used to evoke laughter and can be as important as the verbal punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedians use timing, pause placement, and physicality to enhance or alter the perceived script switch; 'saying things funny' can be more effective than content alone. Consider non-verbal cues in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage incongruity (perception + resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour appreciation involves first the discovery/perception of incongruity and then the resolution of that incongruity; resolution generates laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the joke provides a perceivable incongruity and a plausible resolution in the punchline. Mere incongruity without resolution is insufficient for many verbal jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and context appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes must be tailored to the social situation: narrator, audience, their relationship, and factors such as age, sex, ethnicity, politics, religion, power relations, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify vocabulary, explicitness, and content to fit the audience; the same punchline can be appropriate in one setting and offensive or ineffective in another. Consider social functions (identity, inclusion/exclusion, signalling) when choosing targets and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected response: understanding test (laughter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The expected response to a joke is laughter; a joke functions as an 'understanding test'—if listeners 'get it' they share the intended scripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If audience fails to laugh, they may not recognize the alternate script or may find content objectionable or irrelevant to their tastes/setting. Use testing/audience feedback to gauge success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke cycles: coherence of target and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke cycle is a collection of jokes about a single target or situation that displays consistent narrative structure and type of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise cycles by their repeating SI/TA/NS/LM patterns (e.g., lightbulb jokes, blonde jokes). Cycles arise and spread rapidly, often around topical events; sociocultural analysis considers their function and evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-dimensional classification (GTVH: six KRs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Theory of Verbal Humour (GTVH) proposes six Knowledge Resources (Script Opposition, Logical Mechanism, Situation, Target, Narrative Strategy, Language) that can be evaluated largely independently and concatenated into a label for any joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the six KRs to analyse, compare, and generate jokes; KRs may be hierarchical (some constrain others). The GTVH supports empirical analysis and classification for research and creative recombination of joke elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation sensitivity (puns and language-dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes—especially puns—can be notoriously difficult to translate because they depend on specific words and language features, not just on meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting jokes across languages, check for homophones, idioms, and culture-specific references. Consider rewriting the LM/LA to preserve the script opposition rather than a literal translation of wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orality and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are oral literature that need not be reproduced verbatim; tellers routinely modify text depending on memory and audience while preserving scripts necessary for the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for variant forms and improvisation; successful variants must still support the same divergent scripts and LM. For collection/archival work, note variants and performance contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: post-punchline relief and continuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding material that relieves tension after the punchline or continuing the joke beyond the punchline can undermine the culminating effect and reduce funniness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid immediate explanations, qualifiers, or disclaimers that diffuse the momentum of the punchline. If using a follow-up, ensure it functions as a deliberate tag or escalation rather than dilution.
